profile.summary: 1 Corinthians is a pastoral letter in which Paul responds to an urban church, multiethnic and full of practical tensions. Instead of offering merely pragmatic solutions, he anchors every guidance in the work of Christ, in the grace of God and in the performance of the Spirit. The letter shows how real problems - divisions, sexual morality, processes between brothers, marriage, food sacrificed to idols, public worship, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection - reveal deep convictions about the gospel and the Christian way of life. For the evangelical reader, the book is a valuable portrait of the early church and a permanent guide to discern how faith in Christ shapes relationships, freedom, love and hope.
profile.setting: Corinth was a strategic and prosperous city, located in the isthmus that connected mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with intense flow of travelers and trade between seas and land routes. This position helped make it known for wealth, cultural mix and a broad reputation for immorality. After being destroyed by the Romans and rebuilt as a colony, it became a cosmopolitan center inhabited by Romans, Greeks, Jews, and other Mediterranean groups. The church reflected this environment there: it was young, diverse and marked by internal conflicts. Paul visited her on her second missionary journey, remained about eighteen months and wrote this letter later, during the third trip, probably of Ephesus, around 5356 AD. Pauline authorship is widely accepted, although there is debate about the authenticity of some verses in 14:34-35; the exact date also remains approximate.

structure.label: Greeting and correction of divisions
structure.description: Opening of the letter and response to the formation of groups, the criticism against Paul's way of evangelizing and the problem of human wisdom before the message of the cross.

structure.label: Practical Holiness and Community Discipline
structure.description: Treatment of a serious case of sexual immorality, litigation between siblings and the implications of union with Christ for the body and conduct of the believer.

structure.label: Issues of Christian life in a pagan environment
structure.description: Guidelines on marriage, divorce, loosening, Christian freedom in the face of food sacrificed to idols and the need to consider the good of the other above their own rights.

structure.label: Community life, worship and gifts
structure.description: I teach about roles in the body of Christ, correct use of spiritual gifts, order in worship and the supreme value of Christian love.

structure.label: Resurrection and closure
structure.description: Defense of the resurrection of Christ and the future resurrection of the dead, followed by final instructions and greetings.

themes: The centrality of the cross and the grace of Christ for the whole Christian life
Church unity amid social, cultural and conscious differences
Body and community holiness as a response to the gospel
Christian Freedom Ruled by Sacrificial Love
Spiritual gifts, ordained worship and hope of resurrection
readingKeys: Notice how Paul relates each practical problem to a theological principle, not just with isolated rules.
Realize the tension between Christian freedom and responsibility towards the brother, especially in matters of conscience and testimony.
Read the chapters on love, gifts, and resurrection as the center of Paul's vision for a mature and persevering church.
profile.cautions: The letter deals with concrete situations of a first century church, in an urban and pagan context very different from ours. Pauline authorship is widely accepted, but there is academic debate about some verses of 14:34-35; the date is approximate, usually located between 53 and 56 AD. The introduction does not allow for secure conclusions about details in addition, so it is appropriate to avoid speculation outside this framework.

dossier.narratedEra: The story narrated in 1 Corinthians is set in the city of Corinth, in the Roman province of Acaea, amidst the Greco-Roman world of the 1st century. The letter discusses a newly formed, multi-ethnic church, installed in a strategic port city, marked by trade, international transit, wealth and reputation of immorality.
dossier.compositionEra: The letter was composed by Paul during his third missionary journey, when he was in Ephesus, approximately between A.D. 53 and 56. The notes also place the immediate backdrop in Paul's previous correspondence with Corinth, in the news received from the church and in answers to questions sent by the Corinthians.

politics.title: Corinth as a Roman colony and cosmopolitan city
politics.detail: Corinth was destroyed by the Romans in 146 BC and then rebuilt as a Roman colony. In Paul's time, the city brought together Romans, Greeks, Jews and other Mediterranean groups, as well as international travelers.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the inner divisions of the church as well connected to the mixture of origins, status and habits brought into the Christian community.

politics.title: Corinth under the Roman imperial order
politics.detail: The city was a Roman colony and a strategic point of circulation between the north and south of Greece, as well as connecting maritime routes between the East and the West.
politics.readingImpact: The imperial and colonial context illuminates why the city had economic and social importance, and why a church there could be pressured by public values of status, competition and prestige.

politics.title: Gálio and the Judicial Decision favorable to Paul
politics.detail: During Paul's stay in Corinth, the Jews took him to trial, but the governor Gálio rejected the case for considering him a religious dispute.
politics.readingImpact: This explains the relatively free environment for Paul's evangelization in Corinth and helps to place the birth of the church within a local crisis with Roman authority.

politics.title: Paul's authority in contrast to ministerial rivals
politics.detail: The factions in Corinth identified with Paul, Apollo and Peter, but the notes insist that the leaders do not seem to be in conflict with each other.
politics.readingImpact: The dispute is not treated as personal rivalry between ministers, but as a church problem by absolutizing leadership styles and measuring everything by human criteria.

politics.title: The province of Acaia as an administrative framework
politics.detail: The note identifies Achaea as the division of Greece to which Corinth belonged, and 16:15 calls the house of Stephanas of first converts in the province.
politics.readingImpact: It helps to realize that the Corinthian church was not an isolated case, but was part of a wider regional Christian network.

customs.title: Trade, wealth and urban mobility
customs.detail: Corinth profited from the transit of merchants and travelers crossing the isthmus and with the maritime flow between two gulfs. The city became parade of merchants, including small boats that were pulled by land to avoid dangers of the sea.
customs.readingImpact: This environment helps to understand why the letter touches money, status, ostentation, conflict and attendance to pagan courts: they were plausible pressures of a commercial and competitive society.

customs.title: Reputation of immorality and prostitution
customs.detail: The notes describe Corinth as famous for prostitution and other vices; even a Greek verb attached to the city's name was used to speak of sexual immorality.
customs.readingImpact: This sheds light on Paul's severity at 5:1-13 and 6:12-20, because the church was surrounded by very permissive moral standards.

customs.title: The church was composed mostly of Gentiles, but with some Jews
customs.detail: Matthew Henry says that the church was planted chiefly among the Gentiles, although some Jewish converts were probably present, such as Crispus.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to read Paul's references to pagan practices and idols in 8-10 as something lived by many converts coming directly from paganism.
customs.reference: Matthew Henry's Introduction; 12:2; 1:14; Acts 18:8 (mentioned in note)

customs.title: pagan courts and property disputes
customs.detail: Henry links the avarice and contentions to proceedings between brothers before Gentile judges; the note of 6:1-8 sees in this the use of pagan courts to resolve disputes between believers.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of 6:1-8 is more concrete: Paul deals not only with a legal abstraction, but of a shameful social practice for a community called to witness before non-believers.

customs.title: Meals linked to sacrifices and meat market
customs.detail: In 8:13, the note explains that it was common for pagan temples and sanctuaries to receive animal sacrifices and that the surplus of meat be sold on the market by pagan priests.
customs.readingImpact: The problem ceases to be hypothetical and becomes daily life: what Christians bought or ate could be linked to idolatrous worship, requiring discernment and consideration by the weak brother.

customs.title: The Lord's supper and the Community table
customs.detail: Henry mentions that the rich participated in a scandalous way from the Lord's table, with contempt for the poor brethren.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the deregulation at the Supper involved social differences and humiliation of the poorest, not just liturgical error.

customs.title: Greeting with holy kiss and meeting at home
customs.detail: In 16:20 the note describes the kiss as a common greeting at the time; in 16:19 Aquila and Priscilla gather the church in his house.
customs.readingImpact: It shows the daily life of the early church as domestic and relational, with greeting and meeting practices in homes, not in formal ecclesiastical buildings.

language.title: Language of Greek letters adapted with Christian sense
language.detail: Paul follows the normal pattern of Greek letters in 1:1-3, but magnifies it with Christian significance by introducing apostolate, grace, and peace.
language.readingImpact: The greeting already shapes reading: the letter is not only private correspondence, but speaks of identity, vocation and blessing within faith in Christ.

language.title: -Brothers as a term family and community
language.detail: The note notes that "brothers" in 1:10 is a traditional, generic and affective term addressed to men and women of the same spiritual family.
language.readingImpact: This reinforces that the exhortation to unity is not cold or administrative; Paul speaks as someone seeking reconciliation within a family of faith.

language.title: "Name" and authority
language.detail: In 1:10 the note explains that "name" bears the weight of Christ's authority and reputation.
language.readingImpact: Paul's appeal does not depend on personal prestige, but on the authority of Jesus Christ; this weakens every partisan reading of Christian leadership.

language.title: "Wisdom" and "eloquence" as targets of criticism
language.detail: The notes of 1:17-2:5 and the introduction counterhuman rhetoric to the simple message of the cross. The church valued eloquent words and knowledge, but Paul corrects this self-image.
language.readingImpact: The conflict in Corinth is not only doctrinal, but also cultural: the church was being seduced by criteria of oratory and intellectual sophistication.

language.title: "Knowledge" as slogan and risk of arrogance
language.detail: In 8:1 the expression "all of us" have knowledge" appears as a Corinthian saying, associated with Christians who were judged superior.
language.readingImpact: The phrase reveals a spirituality marked by self-affirmation; Paul responds shifting the focus of knowledge to love and responsibility for the other.

language.title: "Fraco" and "strong" in Christian consciousness
language.detail: In 8:7-13, the note speaks of weak consciousness and of Christians who automatically associated the sacrificed flesh with an act of pagan devotion.
language.readingImpact: Paul is not only regulating food, but dealing with different levels of maturity and the moral impact of Christian freedom on the conscience of others.

language.title: "Grace and peace" as theological formula
language.detail: The note of 1:3 understands grace as an undeserved blessing and peace as well-being rooted in the gospel and produced by the Spirit.
language.readingImpact: The opening already guides the letter to God's graceful action, not for mere practical advice.

timeline.title: 146 BC: destruction of ancient Corinth by the Romans
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the ancient Corinth was conquered and destroyed by Rome in 146 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone explains why Paul's Time Corinth is a rebuilt city, with a much more recent Roman profile than the classical Corinth.

timeline.title: About a century later: reconstruction as Roman colony
timeline.detail: The city was rebuilt approximately a century after its destruction, as already as a Roman colony.
timeline.readingImpact: It helps to read the Christian community within a city with imperial identity and migrant, not as simple continuity of the ancient Greek Corinth.

timeline.title: A.D. 50: Paul's stay in Corinth on the second missionary journey
timeline.detail: The notes place the first arrival of Paul to Corinth on his second missionary journey, with an eighteen-month stay.
timeline.readingImpact: This sets the beginning of the church and shows that many of the problems dealt with in the letter arise a few years after the foundation of the community.

timeline.title: A.D. 5356: writing of 1 Corinthians in Ephesus
timeline.detail: The composition is located during the third missionary journey, in the period of two to three years in Ephesus, approximately AD 53-56.
timeline.readingImpact: The geographical distance between Ephesus and Corinth helps to explain the letter as a pastoral response to reports, visitors and questions received.

timeline.title: After Paul's departure: previous correspondence and later visit
timeline.detail: The introduction says that Paul had already written an earlier letter (1 Cor 5:9), received questions from the Corinthians and also news and visitors of the church; problems still persisted, leading to a later visit and the other letter lost today.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of 1 Corinthians gains a concrete pastoral response character, in dialogue with real crises and not as an isolated treatise.

timeline.title: Immediate context of collection for Jerusalem
timeline.detail: On 16:1-4, the note connects the collection with the churches of Galatia, with Jerusalem and with other Pauline texts, but without fixing an exact date within the chronology of the letter.
timeline.readingImpact: It shows that the letter also participates in a network of cooperation between churches, linking Corinth to the broader needs of the early church.

investigation: The traditional authorship is attributed to Paul; the notes mention a specific academic question about 14:34-35, but do not develop the debate in detail.
The letter is presented as an answer to questions and reports, but the attached sources do not relook in depth each original question or the complete sequence of lost cards.

There is great pastoral and theological emphasis on the notes, but coverage is selective: some themes receive wide attention (unity, cross, idolatry, supper, gifts, resurrection) and others appear only in passing.
Observations on social practices in Corinth are sufficient for contextual reading, but do not constitute independent historical proof outside the material provided itself.
Matthew Henry's notes bring ancient inferences and traditions about certain social details; when this occurs, the basis is interpretive and does not need to be taken as historical certainty.
The sources do not detail the broader political situation of the Roman Empire beyond what is necessary to understand Corinth, Gallius, Achaea, Ephesus and the Pauline travel network.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the notes annexed and therefore does not include external historical or archaeological data. There are real gaps: the local administration of Corinth, the complete chronology of Paul's visits, or the full content of the previous letter lost are not described in depth. There are also controversies mentioned only in a limited way, especially as to 14:34-35 and the identification of some cited persons. At various points, the sources offer pastoral interpretations or plausible inferences; when this occurs, the distinction between explicit affirmation of the source and interpretive reading was maintained. The material favors an evangelical and confessionally conscious perspective, but the dossier seeks to record clearly when the notes only suggest or presuppose something, rather than historically demon.
